title: Gas furnace: safe teardown
summary: A forced-air gas furnace gives a big squirrel-cage blower with its motor and run capacitor, a 24 V control transformer, a control board with relays, an inducer fan, limit switches and a door switch. It is the most dangerous teardown in this set: gas, carbon monoxide, mains power and a hot-surface igniter. Shut off the gas and have the line capped by someone able to do gas work before any gas part comes off; never improvise gas connections, and never fire the furnace again once it has been opened.

steps.text: Stop at the doorway and smell. If you smell gas (rotten eggs), don't go in and don't touch any switch or light, or use a phone, lighter or match, inside the building. Open doors and windows from outside, leave, and let it air for a few hours. If it still smells, leave this furnace alone.
steps.warn: A spark in a room with gas in it can blow up the building. Propane is heavier than air and pools in basements and low spots, and its odorant can fade: no smell does not prove there is no gas.

steps.text: Shut off the gas at the manual shut-off valve on the pipe beside the furnace: turn it so the handle sits across the pipe. Close the meter valve or the propane tank valve too if you can reach it. If the furnace's own valve won't turn, that outer valve is your only shut-off: close it and go no further until the line is capped.
steps.warn: Turn the gas off before the power. Don't force a seized valve: a broken valve can't be closed again.

steps.text: Switch off the power at the furnace's service switch and at its breaker, and lock or tag both. A furnace can have more than one power supply, so check for a second switch or feed.
steps.warn: A generator or solar system wired into the building can keep the furnace live with the grid down.

steps.text: First look at the door edges and any lining or gasket you can see: if it is fibrous, rope-like or papery grey, leave that door on (see safety_asbestos_check). Otherwise take off the upper (burner) door and the lower (blower) door; most lift off hooks or come off with a few screws. Then turn the gas valve's knob or switch to OFF without forcing it.
steps.warn: Pulling the blower door opens a safety switch, but the supply wires stay live until the power is off. Sheet metal edges are sharp: wear gloves. If the furnace ran lately, wait until the burner area and igniter are cool to the touch.

steps.text: Prove it dead. Check your meter on a known live source, then measure between every pair of supply wires in the furnace's junction box and from each to earth. You want no voltage. Then check your meter on the known live source again: if it no longer reads, your zero proved nothing (see safety_mains_isolation).
steps.warn: If anything reads live, stop. Find and switch off the other supply before you touch anything inside.

steps.text: Look before you pull. On old furnaces, especially oil or coal ones, door gaskets and insulation may contain asbestos. Leave any fibrous gasket, rope seal or papery grey wrap undisturbed and work around it (see safety_asbestos_check).

Discharge the blower's run capacitor (a can with two or three terminals, often strapped to the blower housing) and any small capacitor on the inducer with your resistor tool, then check each with your meter (see safety_discharge_capacitor). If the blower motor has a box of electronics on its end (an ECM motor), wait at least 5 minutes and don't open that box.
steps.warn: Goodman's blower capacitors are rated 370 V; read the label on yours. Don't touch the terminals until the meter reads near zero.

steps.text: Cap the gas line before any gas part comes off. The furnace has to be disconnected at the union on its gas pipe (between the shut-off valve and the furnace) and the open pipe sealed with a proper threaded cap or plug, then leak-tested with a leak-detection solution made for gas (not kitchen detergent) or a gas detector. Get someone able to do gas work to do it. If nobody can, leave the gas pipe, gas valve, burners and igniter connected and untouched, and take only the blower, control and inducer parts.
steps.warn: Never leave an open gas pipe. Never improvise a gas fitting with tape, hose, glue or a bung. Never test for gas leaks with a flame.

steps.text: Photograph the wiring and put a tape label on every wire before you unplug anything. Touch bare cabinet metal before handling the control board to drain static from your body.

Take the control board: squeeze each harness plug's latch and pull the plug, not the wires, then undo its screws or clips and lift it out. Take the 24 V transformer from the control box (undo its mounting screws and label its wires) and the small 24 V circuit breaker if there is one.
Blower: unplug the motor's wires, undo the screws that hold the blower housing in the cabinet, and slide the whole housing out with the motor and wheel inside it.
steps.warn: The blower assembly is heavy and awkward. Support it as it clears its rails; keep fingers out from under it.

steps.text: On the bench, loosen the set screw on the blower wheel's hub, undo the motor mount bolts and slide the motor out of the wheel. Keep the run capacitor and its strap with the motor, and twist a bare wire across its terminals for storage (see safety_discharge_capacitor).

Inducer (the small motor and fan on the flue collector box in the upper compartment): unplug it, pull the small rubber tube off the pressure switch beside it, undo its screws and lift it off with its gasket. Take the pressure switch too.
steps.warn: Once the inducer or any flue part is off, this furnace must never be fired again: fumes would spill into the building, and carbon monoxide kills.

steps.text: Only if the gas line has been capped and leak-tested by someone able to do gas work: unplug the igniter and the flame sensor and take each off the burner assembly (one or two screws each). Leave the gas valve, the gas pipe, the manifold and the burners where they are: taking them off means breaking gas joints.
steps.warn: Hold the hot-surface igniter by its base only. Never touch its element and don't knock it: it is brittle and breaks easily, and it stays hot after use.

steps.text: Take the limit switches, the rollout switches and the door switch: each comes off with one or two screws. Then tag the cabinet and the shut-off valve (and the cap, if the pipe was capped): "Gas off. Furnace stripped. Do not open this valve, reconnect or light."

notes:
## Gas and carbon monoxide first

- Both makers say installation and service must be done by a qualified installer, service agency or the gas supplier (Goodman IO-359J; Lennox 1120). This guide keeps to that: if nobody able to cap the gas line is around, the gas side stays connected, closed and untouched.
- The installer fits a manual shut-off valve, a ground-joint union and a drip leg ahead of the furnace, with the union downstream of the shut-off valve (Goodman IO-359J). That union is where the furnace comes off and the pipe gets capped.
- Check every gas joint with a leak-detection solution made for gas, or a gas detector (Goodman specifies chloride-free soap and water; Lennox warns that kitchen detergent can corrode gas pipework). Never use a match or flame (Goodman IO-359J; Lennox 1120).
- If the furnace overheats or the gas won't shut off, close the manual shut-off valve before cutting the power (Goodman IO-359J).
- Carbon monoxide can cause serious illness, permanent brain damage or death, and a badly repaired furnace can make it (Goodman IO-359J). A furnace that has been opened for salvage is never to be fired again. See safety_carbon_monoxide before you heat any shelter with fuel.
- Don't take the gas valve, manifold or burners off yourself: that means breaking gas joints, which the makers leave to a qualified installer or service agency. A gas valve that has been taken off is never to go back on a gas line.

## What's worth keeping and why

- **Blower motor and wheel.** Many are permanent split capacitor (PSC) motors with several speeds. The Rheem R801P uses a 4-speed PSC motor of 1/3 hp (248 W) to 3/4 hp (560 W) by size, on 115 V (Rheem R801P spec); the Goodman GMS8 lists 4-speed motors of 1/3 and 1/2 hp and a 3/4 hp motor by size (Goodman RP-855C). With its wheel it moves a lot of air: shelter ventilation, a drying room or workshop cooling, wherever mains power exists. The motor label or wiring diagram shows which wire gives which speed; power one speed wire at a time, always with its run capacitor (skill_read_nameplate).
- **ECM blower motors.** Some furnaces use an electronically commutated motor instead. The Lennox ML180UHE has a constant-torque ECM on 120 V. Each of its five speed taps is switched on by 24 V AC; the motor is not field repairable, and each replacement control module is made for one motor size (Lennox 1120). ECM controls are factory programmed for their equipment (ClimateMaster ECM). To reuse one, keep its plugs and the furnace's transformer and run it the way the furnace did.
- **Run capacitor.** The Goodman GMS8 uses 12.5, 20 or 25 µF capacitors rated 370 V, by furnace size (Goodman RP-855C). Keep it with its motor; it is also a spare for any PSC motor that calls for the same value (test_capacitor).
- **Control transformer.** 120 V in, 24 V AC out, rated 40 VA (Goodman RP-855C; Lennox 1120): about 1.7 A at 24 V. It powers 24 V AC relays, zone and irrigation valves and thermostat circuits (teardown_wall_thermostat).
- **Control board.** Relays, a small fuse or breaker, connectors and LEDs. The Lennox integrated control is not field repairable, so take it for parts (Lennox 1120). Read each relay's coil voltage and contact rating on its case before reuse.
- **Inducer.** A 120 V motor with a small blower wheel that moves air through the burners and heat exchanger (Lennox 1120); some have their own small capacitor (Goodman RP-855C). It makes a good blower for a forge or stove (build_brake_drum_forge).
- **Pressure switch.** A diaphragm switch that closes on a small suction, set in inches of water column (Lennox 1120). Use it to prove a blower is running.
- **Limit and rollout switches.** Snap-disc thermal switches. The Lennox has two rollout switches, normally closed with a manual reset and a fixed setpoint of 210 °F (99 °C) (Lennox 1120). The Rheem lists a main limit, manual-reset limits in the burner compartment and a limit in the blower housing (Rheem R801P parts). Read the temperature marked on each one before you trust it; the Lennox primary limit has a different setpoint for each model (Lennox 1120). A switch whose rating you can't read is not a safe over-heat cut-out for a heater or stove fan.
- **Door switch.** The Lennox one is rated 14 A at 125 V AC (Lennox 1120): a sturdy push switch.
- **Igniter and flame sensor.** Spares for a matching appliance repaired by someone trained, nothing more. The Lennox nitride hot-surface igniter reads 39–70 Ω and runs on 120 V (Lennox 1120); the Goodman one should read no more than 75 Ω at about 21 °C (70 °F) (Goodman IO-359J). Rheem's R801P uses a spark ignitor instead (Rheem R801P parts). The flame sensor is a probe that proves the flame by flame rectification (Goodman IO-359J).
- **Gas valve.** The Lennox valve is internally redundant, with a pressure regulator and 24 V AC terminals (Lennox 1120). Leave it on the burner assembly: taking it off means breaking gas joints, which is a gas fitter's job (see above).

## Testing what you got out

- **PSC motor:** spin it by hand, then check the windings and insulation (test_motor).
- **Capacitor:** test_capacitor.
- **Transformer:** check both windings for continuity and look for about 24 V AC out with 120 V in, through a dim-bulb tester first (test_transformer).
- **Igniter:** measure its resistance against the figures above. A cracked igniter is scrap.

## Variations

- The three furnaces logged here are 80 % gas furnaces with an inducer: Goodman GMS8, Lennox ML180UHE and Rheem R801P. Oil, electric (240 V heating elements) and condensing furnaces differ and are not covered: check yours before following these steps.
- Blower: PSC motor and capacitor (Goodman, Rheem) or ECM (Lennox).
- Ignition: hot-surface (Goodman, Lennox) or spark (Rheem).
- Fuel: units ship for natural gas, and kits convert them to propane (Lennox 1120). Check the label: propane pools low.
- Weight: shipping weights run about 85–150 lb (39–68 kg) for the R801P (Rheem R801P spec) and 111–178 lb (50–81 kg) for the ML180UHE (Lennox 1120). Strip it where it stands.

## What to leave

- The heat exchanger. It is aluminized steel (Lennox 1120; Rheem R801P spec), and getting it out means taking out the burner assembly and may mean spreading the cabinet (Lennox 1120). Heavy, awkward and low value.
- The whole gas side: gas valve, gas pipe, manifold and burners. Leave them where they are.
- Anything that may contain asbestos. The EPA lists oil and coal furnaces and their door gaskets among places asbestos insulation may be found (EPA asbestos).
- The inside of an ECM motor's control box.
- The furnace itself as a heater. Never refire it.
